**I.	INTRODUCTION**

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a condition where the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste from the blood. This damage builds up over months and years, often without any warning signs. By the time a person feels sick, the disease may already be in an advanced stage. According to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, published in The Lancet, approximately 788 million adults worldwide had CKD in 2023 — more than double the 378 million recorded in 1990.\[1\] The disease was the ninth leading cause of death globally, responsible for approximately 1.48 million deaths in 2023.\[1\]

One of the biggest problems with CKD is that most people do not know they have it. Globally, only about 10% of those at risk were aware of their condition.\[3\] Since the disease shows no clear symptoms in its early stages, most patients only find out when their kidneys have already suffered serious and permanent damage. This makes early detection critical — and yet it remains rare in many parts of the world.

In the Philippines, the problem is far worse than the global average. A study published in the Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific (2023) found that CKD prevalence in the Philippines was 35.94% — nearly three times the global rate.\[4\] Based on a national population of 115.6 million, this translated to an estimated 12.94 million Filipinos living with some stage of CKD.\[5\] The National Kidney and Transplant Institute (NKTI) reported that one Filipino developed chronic kidney failure every hour, equivalent to approximately 120 new cases per million population annually, and that the condition remained largely underdiagnosed across the country.\[9,38\] By 2019, kidney disease had already ranked as the fourth leading cause of death in the country.\[7\]

The financial cost of CKD in the Philippines has been growing rapidly. The number of Filipinos undergoing dialysis jumped from 53,296 in 2023 to 64,845 in 2024 — a 22% increase in just one year.\[9\] Kidney failure was identified as the second largest expense of PhilHealth, the country's national health insurer.\[10\] Each patient on dialysis may receive up to PHP 990,600 in annual PhilHealth coverage, yet out-of-pocket costs remain a heavy burden for many Filipino families.\[11\] The main causes of CKD in the Philippines were kidney damage from high blood pressure (33.07%) and diabetes (30.04%) — both of which are preventable with early action.\[9\]

The situation in Davao City and Region XI reflects the national crisis at a local level. Since 2017, Davao City has ranked third in the Philippines for the number of kidney disease patients.\[14\] As of 2022, the region had approximately 2,400 patients on dialysis, growing at a rate of 12 to 15 percent each year.\[15\] By late 2025, that number had risen to approximately 3,000.\[16\] At the Southern Philippines Medical Center (SPMC) alone, around 200 kidney patients were seen daily.\[16\]

In response to the growing burden of CKD, several digital health tools have been developed to support kidney disease awareness and management. These include mobile applications, clinical screening tools, and online questionnaires available globally and locally. In the Philippines, the Philippine Society of Nephrology (PSN) launched its \#StopCKD initiative, which offered a free online self-assessment quiz based on the SCORED model.\[8\] AstraZeneca Philippines also released a printed SCORED questionnaire card under an AMA content license (License No. 5263480664527, March 7, 2022\) for distribution to Filipino patients.\[21\] These efforts showed a growing recognition that screening tools need to reach Filipinos beyond the walls of a hospital.

However, a closer look at available tools reveals significant gaps. Table 1 compares several existing CKD-related tools across five key features: whether they target the general public, whether they require laboratory tests, whether they use a validated screening instrument, whether they use a conversational interface, and whether they were designed for the Filipino context.

As shown in the table, most existing tools were built for clinical use and required laboratory results such as eGFR or serum creatinine — tests that many Filipinos have never had.\[22\] Tools like Kidney Choices were designed for patients already diagnosed with CKD, not for those who are unaware of their risk.\[22\] While the SCORED questionnaire card remained accessible as a static document through the AstraZeneca Philippines repository \[21\], the PSN's \#StopCKD interactive screening platform was no longer active at the time this study was conducted, and no peer-reviewed study had documented its reach or effectiveness \[8\].

The gap is clear: there is no existing tool that combines a validated, PSN-endorsed CKD screening instrument with a design made specifically for Filipino adults who have no laboratory results and no prior CKD diagnosis. Most tools are either too clinical, too foreign, or no longer active. Filipino adults at risk have no simple, accessible way to check their kidney health on their own.

Beyond the lack of a Filipino-specific screening tool, there is another gap worth noting: no chatbot-based CKD risk screening system exists for the Filipino general public. While chatbot technology has been used in other areas of health — such as mental health support and general symptom checking — no equivalent tool has been developed or published for CKD risk detection in the Philippines.\[25\] This represents a missed opportunity, given how widely Filipinos use smartphones and messaging applications for daily communication.

Chatbots are particularly well-suited for health screening because they deliver questions in a conversational, step-by-step format that feels familiar and less intimidating than a clinical form.\[25\] Studies conducted in the Philippine context have demonstrated that users responded positively to chatbot-based health tools, reporting high satisfaction and acceptance of conversational interfaces for health assessment purposes \[34, 35\]. Beyond user preference, comparative studies have shown that chatbot-delivered health assessments provided superior engagement and intuitiveness compared to standard online forms, particularly in scenarios where sustained attention and comprehension were required \[36, 37\]. These findings are especially relevant to CKD risk screening, which involves multiple variables and medical terminology that may not be readily understood by the general public \[20\]. By structuring the assessment as a guided, step-by-step interaction, chatbot interfaces reduced cognitive burden and helped maintain user participation throughout the screening process \[36, 37\]. This made them well-suited for conditions like CKD, where low public awareness and the absence of early symptoms have historically contributed to poor engagement with conventional screening approaches \[1, 3\].

In response to these gaps, the researchers will develop BATO: Bridging Awareness Through Online Risk Assessment — a web-based system comprising two distinct chatbot subsystems that together enable Filipino adults to assess their CKD risk and access reliable CKD health information through a simple online interface. The system name BATO is derived from the Filipino colloquial term for kidney — the organ is commonly referred to as "bato," literally "stone," owing to its characteristic stone-like shape. This name was intentionally adopted as a backronym, following the naming convention of the SCORED instrument itself (SCreening for Occult REnal Disease), in which letters were selected for clinical resonance rather than strict positional mapping to each word. "Bato" was prioritized over a mechanically derived acronym to maximize immediate recognizability and cultural relevance among the study's target population of Filipino adults, consistent with health literacy and social value considerations in the study's ethical framework.

The first subsystem is the Risk Assessment Chatbot, which administers the SCORED (SCreening for Occult REnal Disease) model by Bang et al. (2007) — a nine-variable, non-laboratory screening tool.\[20\] AstraZeneca obtained an AMA content license (No. 5263480664527, 03/07/2022) for the SCORED instrument, which was distributed in the Philippines and subsequently promoted by the PSN through its \#StopCKD public awareness campaign by directing Filipinos to the licensed questionnaire as early as March 2023, demonstrating practical institutional application of the instrument in the Philippine healthcare context despite the absence of formal validation studies in Filipino populations.\[8, 21, 38\]. Based on the user's answers, the Risk Assessment Chatbot will compute a total risk score and classify the result as either Screen Negative (score of 0 to 3\) or Screen Positive (score of 4 and above), consistent with the single recommended cutoff established by Bang et al. (2007), with a sensitivity of 92% and a negative predictive value of 99% at this threshold.\[20\] Users who score 4 and above will be informed of an elevated likelihood of CKD and advised to consult a physician for confirmatory testing, while users who score 0 to 3 will be advised that they are likely not at risk at present but will be encouraged to retake the assessment at least once a year. At any point during the assessment, users may ask the chatbot to clarify unfamiliar clinical terms. These clarification requests are answered through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): the user's question is embedded and matched against a vector database of pre-approved content drawn from official health organizations, clinical practice guidelines, and peer-reviewed literature, and only the passages retrieved under the screening-clarification scope are supplied to the language model, which returns a plain-language explanation before the rule-based controller resumes the current screening variable. Retrieval scope is enforced server-side rather than through instructions given to the language model, and the language model has no access to, and no influence over, the scoring computation.

The second subsystem is the General CKD Chatbot, a free-form conversational assistant that allows users to ask open-ended questions about CKD causes, symptoms, risk factors, prevention, and management at any point in their engagement with the system. Like the Risk Assessment Chatbot's LLM Clarification Engine, the General CKD Chatbot is grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), drawing on the same shared vector database of pre-approved content. The two subsystems are distinguished not by their grounding mechanism but by their retrieval scope: the Risk Assessment Chatbot retrieves only from passages scoped to screening-variable clarification, while the General CKD Chatbot retrieves across the full general CKD education corpus. In both cases, only the most relevant retrieved passages are used to generate a response, with every claim traceable to its source. A scope guardrail restricts the chatbot to CKD-related topics and deflects both off-topic and adversarial (prompt-injection) queries before retrieval occurs. The General CKD Chatbot carries no scoring logic and has no defined endpoint, making it a complementary resource for users who wish to learn more about CKD beyond the structured assessment. Both chatbots are accessible from the main landing page via two distinct entry points.

Beyond delivering the screening result, BATO addresses the step that follows it. Users who screen positive are advised to seek confirmatory testing, but the absence of a clear and proximate destination is itself a barrier to follow-through, particularly for users who have never previously engaged with kidney care services. BATO therefore includes a Facility Locator that links users to nearby Department of Health–licensed clinical laboratories where the serum creatinine test indicated by the SCORED instrument can be obtained. The directory is deliberately confined to confirmatory testing rather than specialist nephrology care: at the recommended cutoff of four or higher, the instrument carries a positive predictive value of 18 percent, meaning that most users receiving a Screen Positive result will not have chronic kidney disease, and directing them toward specialist or renal replacement services would overstate what a non-laboratory screening questionnaire is able to establish \[20\]. With the user's explicit permission, the system resolves the device's approximate location — or accepts a manually entered city or municipality where permission is withheld — and displays the nearest laboratories on an interactive digital map drawn from a curated directory compiled from the DOH National Health Facility Registry. Location input is used solely to generate the result set for the current session and is neither stored nor logged by the system. The facility listing is informational and does not constitute an endorsement, a clinical referral, or a guarantee of service availability; an accompanying disclaimer directs users to confirm test availability and operating hours directly with the facility before travelling.

While SCORED was designed as a non-laboratory screening instrument, several of its nine variables presupposed prior clinical or laboratory knowledge. Conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, heart attack, stroke, heart failure, and anemia — though requiring prior medical diagnosis or laboratory testing — were considered more likely to be recognized by Filipino adults who had already been diagnosed, as patients with these conditions are more commonly informed of their status through routine clinical encounters and community health programs \[29, 30\]. 

In contrast, PVD and proteinuria presented a compounded challenge — not only do both conditions require clinical or laboratory procedures for detection, but public awareness of each has been documented to be markedly low. Studies have consistently shown that awareness of PVD among the general public is substantially lower than that of conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, and stroke; one population-based survey found that while awareness of high blood pressure reached 89.7%, diabetes 77%, and stroke 73.9%, only 25% of respondents reported any familiarity with peripheral arterial disease \[31\]. On an international level, this gap persisted, with 57% of general population respondents reporting being 'not at all familiar' with PVD \[32\]. 

Similarly, proteinuria is typically asymptomatic and produces no recognizable signs that a lay user could identify without prior medical testing, with public awareness of the condition documented as low even among populations with known CKD risk factors \[33\]. A lay Filipino user encountering these two questions without prior clinical evaluation would therefore face both a knowledge gap — not knowing their status — and a comprehension gap — not understanding what the question is asking. To address this, prior to the screening sequence, BATO will inform users that any statement that is uncertain or inapplicable should be recorded as zero — consistent with the guidance provided on the officially licensed AstraZeneca Philippines patient card \[21\]. Unlike a static questionnaire, BATO's LLM-powered chatbot will allow users to submit clarifying questions at any point during the screening, with the system retrieving the relevant passages from the approved knowledge base and returning a plain-language response grounded in that retrieved material before resuming the current SCORED variable. This capability is of particular relevance to the PVD and proteinuria questions, where lay comprehension and public awareness have been documented as low \[28, 31, 32, 33\]; users who are uncertain about either condition will be able to request an explanation from the chatbot and receive a response before recording their answer, without disrupting the sequence of the assessment. 

Bang et al. (2007) conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding both anemia and PVD from the prediction model and found only marginal reduction in accuracy, with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve decreasing from 0.88 to 0.87, indicating that the instrument retained strong discriminative performance even when these clinically dependent variables were unavailable \[20\]. Bang et al. also conducted a sensitivity analysis excluding individuals with proteinuria from the development set and eliminating it as an independent variable, finding that the model fit changed only marginally, with the AUC declining from 0.88 to 0.878 — consistent with the minimal attenuation observed when anemia and PVD were omitted \[20\]. This indicates that the instrument retained strong discriminative performance even without proteinuria as an active variable. Separately, Bang et al. acknowledged that self-reported proteinuria may not be reliable and is often not assessed, even among high-risk populations \[20\]. Together, these findings suggest that while proteinuria contributes meaningfully to the model, its uncertain self-report in the context of BATO does not critically undermine the instrument's screening performance. Nevertheless, the handling of proteinuria under conditions of user uncertainty will be identified as a limitation of the current implementation of BATO, and the embedding of automatic plain-language clarification for this variable will be noted as a direction for future improvement.

BATO aims to offer benefits at multiple levels. For individual users, it seeks to provide a fast and free way to assess their kidney health risk without requiring a hospital visit or laboratory test, and to identify where nearby that risk can be confirmed through professional evaluation. For communities — particularly in Davao Region, where dialysis cases had been rising at 12 to 15 percent annually and access to formal CKD screening remained limited — BATO aims to extend the reach of evidence-based CKD screening to Filipino adults who might otherwise never be assessed \[15, 39\]. At the institutional level, BATO will support the DOH's CKD prevention mandate and the PSN's public awareness goals. At the research level, it aims to contribute evidence on whether a chatbot-based approach to CKD risk screening was feasible, usable, and acceptable in a Filipino community setting — a question that no prior published study had yet answered.

1. **Objectives of  the  Study**  
   The general objective of this study is to design, develop, and evaluate BATO: a web-based conversational system comprising two chatbot subsystems and a facility locator that will enable Filipino adults to self-assess their risk for Chronic Kidney Disease using the internationally validated and PSN-promoted SCORED prediction model, without requiring laboratory tests or clinical consultation.  
   Specifically, this study aims to:  
1. Develop a risk assessment model that calculates CKD risk using the nine variables of the SCORED Model.  
2. Design and implement two AI-powered chatbot subsystems: a Risk Assessment Chatbot that facilitates intuitive, user-guided SCORED screening, and a General CKD Chatbot that provides reliable, source-grounded health education.  
3. Implement a facility locator that links users to nearby DOH-licensed clinical laboratories offering serum creatinine testing through an interactive digital map.  
4. Evaluate system usability using the System Usability Testing (SUS) and assess user acceptance and medical trust using the TAM and TiMT framework.

**II.	METHODS AND MATERIALS**

1. **Research Method**  
   This study will employ applied developmental research, as it is directed toward the design, development, and evaluation of a functional technology-based system intended to address a clearly identified public health gap. The software development process will follow the Agile Software Development Methodology, organized into eight iterative sprints. Agile was selected because BATO’s core components — the SCORED scoring engine, chatbot interface, recommendation engine, and educational content system — are best built and validated incrementally, and the sprint structure will accommodate continuous adviser feedback and allow for refinement at each stage of development.  
   The system will be developed using React as the front-end framework and Supabase as the back-end platform. React was selected for its component-based architecture, which supports modular and maintainable UI development and enables the dynamic, real-time interaction patterns required by BATO's conversational chatbot interface. Supabase was selected as the back-end platform because it provides a PostgreSQL-based relational database with native pgvector support for vector similarity search, serverless Edge Functions for secure server-side execution, and built-in Row Level Security (RLS) — features directly relevant to BATO's shared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, its curated facility directory, and the enforcement of read-only, server-mediated access to all stored content. Together, these technologies provide a scalable and maintainable full-stack foundation within the project's development timeline.  
   BATO does not require user registration or authentication. The SCORED assessment is a point-in-time screening whose output is delivered immediately within the same session, and no element of the statement of the problem depends on the longitudinal tracking of an identified individual. Consistent with the data minimization principle of Republic Act No. 10173, the Data Privacy Act of 2012, which requires that collected data be limited to what is directly necessary for the declared purpose, the system therefore creates no user accounts, collects no personally identifiable information, and does not persist assessment responses or results beyond the active session. Removing the account layer additionally lowers the barrier to entry for the target population, for whom a registration requirement would constitute an unnecessary point of abandonment before any screening value is delivered.  
   BATO will feature two distinct chatbot subsystems, each accessible from the main landing page via a dedicated button. The first is the Risk Assessment Chatbot, which administers the SCORED screening instrument. This chatbot employs a hybrid architecture: a rule-based controller governs the strict sequential presentation of the nine SCORED variables and is solely responsible for computing the final risk score, while a large language model (LLM) serves a strictly bounded supporting role limited to clarifying and simplifying clinical terminology when the user requests it. For example, if a user is uncertain about what peripheral vascular disease or proteinuria means, they may ask the chatbot. The request is then handled through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): the question is embedded and matched against a shared vector database of pre-approved content assembled under the source inclusion framework described below, and only the passages retrieved under the screening-clarification scope are passed to the LLM, which generates a plain-language explanation restricted to that retrieved material. Because retrieval for this subsystem is confined to terminology definitions and is filtered by scope in the Edge Function before the LLM is invoked, the clarification branch cannot introduce content capable of reinterpreting, reframing, or otherwise influencing the value recorded for any SCORED variable. Where content is drawn from clinical practice guidelines or peer-reviewed literature, it will be simplified for lay comprehension before it is chunked, embedded, and indexed into the shared vector store, with the simplified text retained alongside a citation to its original source. The LLM has no role in scoring computation and cannot influence the values recorded for any SCORED variable. The rule-based controller resumes the assessment after each clarification exchange, and all nine variables must be answered before a risk score is computed, preserving the integrity of the validated instrument. The conversation has a defined endpoint: the display of the SCORED result and corresponding health recommendation. The second is the General CKD Chatbot, a free-form conversational assistant whose topical boundary is enforced at the Edge Function layer, which evaluates each incoming query for CKD relevance before retrieval is performed and declines out-of-scope and adversarial inputs without invoking retrieval or generation. It follows no fixed sequence and has no scoring logic or defined endpoint, allowing users to ask open-ended questions about CKD causes, symptoms, prevention, and management at any stage of their engagement with the system. Like the Risk Assessment Chatbot, its responses are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation over the same shared vector store of pre-approved content, with the two subsystems separated by scope metadata within a single pipeline rather than by separate infrastructures, ensuring that all information provided remains source-attributable and institutionally credible. Both chatbots share a common React chat UI component and route their requests through shared Supabase Edge Functions, which perform query embedding, scope-filtered vector retrieval, and the LLM call entirely server-side. This arrangement ensures that API credentials are never exposed in the client-side build, and that the scope separating the two subsystems is enforced structurally within the retrieval query rather than through instructions given to the language model.  
   The knowledge base that grounds both chatbots is assembled under a defined source inclusion framework rather than a fixed enumeration, so that coverage can be extended over the course of development without weakening the accountability chain required of a health screening tool. Eligible sources fall into three categories. The first is official health organizations and government health agencies, including the Philippine Society of Nephrology (PSN), the Department of Health (DOH), the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), and AstraZeneca Philippines in its capacity as the licensed publisher of the SCORED patient questionnaire in the Philippines. The second is clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements issued by recognized nephrology and allied clinical bodies, including Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO). The third is peer-reviewed journal literature published in journals indexed in established bibliographic databases and subject to editorial peer review.  
   Sources are admitted only where authorship is institutionally or editorially attributable, where the content is current — defined as the prevailing edition of a guideline, or publication within the last ten years for journal literature unless the work is a foundational reference for the instrument itself — and where the material is publicly retrievable for verification. Grey literature, commercial health portals, patient forums, promotional material, unindexed or predatory journals, and any content that cannot be traced to a named institutional or editorial authority are excluded. Every candidate source is reviewed and approved by the adviser before ingestion, and each ingested chunk carries provenance metadata recording its source, category, and publication or revision year, so that any statement produced by either chatbot can be traced to an accountable origin.  
   Complementing the two chatbot subsystems, the Facility Locator is a non-conversational module that presents nearby clinical laboratories on an interactive digital map. It draws on a curated facility directory stored in Supabase, compiled from the DOH National Health Facility Registry and filtered to records of the Clinical Laboratory facility type holding a current licensing status within Region XI. The directory is further restricted to laboratories of Level 2 and Level 3 service capability, as Department of Health Administrative Order No. 2021-0037 establishes routine clinical chemistry — the category under which blood creatinine falls — as a required service capability beginning at Level 2, while Level 1 laboratories are not required to offer it and no inference of availability can therefore be drawn from a Level 1 designation. Records carrying no published service capability are excluded pending individual verification, as they may belong to specialised licence categories such as drug testing or newborn screening laboratories rather than general clinical laboratories. Each entry records the health facility code, facility name, ownership classification, service capability level, address, barangay and its PSGC code, city or municipality, province, geographic coordinates, licensing status and validity date where published, and the date on which the record was captured. Because the registry does not publish geographic coordinates, each facility is located at the representative point of its barangay, obtained by joining the record's ten-digit PSGC code to a barangay boundary dataset derived from NAMRIA administrative-boundary shapefiles and the PSA Philippine Standard Geographic Code \[45, 46, 47\]. Multi-part barangays are dissolved by PSGC code before the representative point is computed, so that every point falls within the barangay it represents rather than in the interval between discontinuous parts. All 256 Region XI facility records resolved against this dataset without exception, and a sample of the resulting coordinates is verified by manual spot-check before ingestion. Proximity is computed server-side against either the device's approximate coordinates, obtained only through the browser geolocation permission prompt at the point of use, or a city or municipality entered manually by the user; neither is written to the database or to application logs. The directory is maintained as a dated snapshot rather than a live feed, with the capture date displayed alongside the results, and map rendering is performed using digital map service. The module is invoked only after a risk classification has been produced, or independently from the landing page, and it is architecturally separate from the screening flow: it receives the classification as a display parameter but returns no value to the Rule-Based Screening Controller, the SCORED Scoring Engine, or the Risk Classification Module, and therefore cannot influence the computed score or its interpretation.  
   The geographic boundary of the facility directory was determined empirically rather than assumed. A nationwide extract of Clinical Laboratory records was obtained from the National Health Facility Registry, comprising 4,318 records of which 4,301 held a current licence at the time of capture. Applying the service capability inclusion rule to this national extract retained 254 laboratories, or 5.9 percent, of which 131 were located in Region XI. Service capability was recorded in only four of the eighteen regions represented, with fourteen regions — including Central Luzon at 855 licensed laboratories and CALABARZON at 639 — carrying no recorded capability for any laboratory. Because the registry publishes a distinct service capability value for drug testing laboratories where that classification applies, these blanks reflect unpopulated fields rather than specialised licence categories. Region XI was consequently retained as the directory boundary, being the region in which the registry supports the inclusion rule at usable completeness.  
   **Conceptual Framework**  
   The conceptual framework of BATO follows an Input-Process-Output (IPO) model describing the logical flow of data and operations within the system. Because BATO comprises two distinct chatbot subsystems, each with a different operational structure, the framework is presented as two separate IPO diagrams one for the Risk Assessment Chatbot and one for the General CKD Chatbot.  
   **Risk Assessment Chatbot**  
   	The Input layer consists of the conversational session data generated during the screening process, which includes the user's binary responses to the nine SCORED variables — age bracket, biological sex, anemia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, history of cardiovascular disease, history of congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, and proteinuria — as well as any clarifying questions submitted by the user during the screening session. Where the user elects to use the Facility Locator, the Input layer additionally receives an optional location input, supplied either as device coordinates through the browser geolocation permission prompt or as a manually entered city or municipality. No account credentials are collected, as the system operates without user registration.  
   The Process layer consists of four components. First, the Rule-Based Screening Controller governs the strict sequential presentation of the nine SCORED variables, enforces the session completion condition requiring all nine variables to be answered before scoring proceeds, and maps each confirmed user response to its corresponding binary or categorical SCORED value. When the user submits a clarifying question, the controller delegates to the LLM Clarification Engine, which operates as a retrieval-augmented side branch outside the scoring path: the question is embedded, matched against the shared vector store of approved content under a scope filter that restricts retrieval to screening-clarification passages, and answered using only the retrieved material. If no retrieved passage meets the similarity threshold, the engine declines to answer rather than generating unsupported content. Control then returns to the Rule-Based Screening Controller to resume the current variable. This branch can neither record nor modify the value of any SCORED variable. Second, upon session completion, the SCORED Scoring Engine applies the weighted scoring rubric from Bang et al. (2007) to the collected binary responses to compute a cumulative risk score. Third, the Risk Classification Module categorizes the score as Screen Negative (0–3) or Screen Positive (≥4) and triggers the Recommendation Engine, which retrieves the appropriate health guidance and educational content corresponding to the user's classification. Fourth, the Facility Locator Module may be invoked at the user's election following classification; where an optional location input is supplied, it queries the curated facility directory for the nearest licensed clinical laboratories offering serum creatinine testing and prepares them for display on an interactive digital map. This module is invoked after classification and returns no value to any preceding component, and therefore cannot affect the computed score or its classification.  
   The Output layer presents the user with their SCORED risk classification, personalized health recommendations, relevant CKD educational content drawn from the approved source corpus, an optional map view of nearby clinical laboratories where the recommended serum creatinine test can be obtained, and a medical disclaimer stating that BATO is a screening tool only and not a substitute for clinical diagnosis, accompanied by a facility disclaimer clarifying that the listing is informational and does not constitute an endorsement or clinical referral.  
   The deterministic components execute in strict sequence: the Rule-Based Screening Controller collects all nine variable responses before passing them to the SCORED Scoring Engine, whose output feeds directly into the Risk Classification Module, whose classification then triggers the Recommendation Engine to produce a unified result set delivered to the Output layer. Two components sit outside this sequence. The LLM Clarification Engine is a side branch invoked mid-assessment and returns control to the Rule-Based Screening Controller without writing to any variable, while the Facility Locator Module is invoked only after classification and returns no value to any upstream component. Neither is capable of altering the score or the classification, preserving the determinism of the validated instrument.

![][image1]

*Figure 1: BATO Risk Assessment Diagram*

**General CKD Chatbot**

The Input layer consists of free-form conversational input submitted by the user, which may include questions about CKD causes, symptoms, risk factors, prevention strategies, and disease management. No account credentials are collected, as the system operates without user registration.

The Process layer consists of two components. First, the Scope Guardrail, implemented at the Supabase Edge Function layer, evaluates each incoming query for CKD relevance and declines off-topic and adversarial (prompt-injection) inputs before any retrieval or generation occurs. Second, the Retrieval-Augmented Conversation Engine embeds the accepted query, performs a similarity search against the shared vector store of approved content under the general CKD education scope filter, and generates a plain-language response using only the retrieved passages, with each claim attributable to its source document. Where no retrieved passage meets the similarity threshold, the system declines to answer rather than generating unsupported content. There is no scoring logic, no fixed variable sequence, and no defined session endpoint.

The Output layer presents the user with a source-grounded, plain-language conversational response to their query. No risk classification or scoring output is produced by this subsystem.

![][image2]

*Figure 2: BATO General CKD Chatbot Diagram*

The scope of BATO will be bounded to Filipino adults aged 20 and above, operating exclusively as a non-clinical risk screening tool. The system operates without user accounts and does not retain assessment responses or results after a session ends. The facility directory served by the Facility Locator will be limited to DOH-licensed clinical laboratories within Davao Region (Region XI). This boundary reflects the study's evaluation setting and, more decisively, the completeness of the underlying registry: a nationwide extract of Clinical Laboratory records showed that the service capability field on which the inclusion rule depends is populated in only four of eighteen regions, with Region XI the most complete at 51.6 percent of licensed laboratories, against fourteen regions in which no laboratory carries a recorded service capability at all. A national directory could not therefore apply the inclusion rule without either returning no results across most of the country or admitting laboratories whose capability is unknown. Specialist nephrology and renal replacement facilities are outside its scope, as confirmatory testing rather than specialist referral is the action the instrument recommends at the screening stage. The system will be delivered as a web-based application built with React and Supabase, across the two-term academic timeline of Capstone 1 and Capstone 2\.

2. **Design Procedure**  
   The development of BATO will follow eight Agile sprints. Each sprint will produce a verifiable system increment reviewed by the adviser before the next sprint begins.

![][image3]*Figure 3:  Agile Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)*

**Sprint 1: Requirements Analysis and System Design**

This sprint will establish the full technical blueprint of BATO prior to development. Key tasks:

* Finalize functional and non-functional requirements mapped to the four study objectives  
* Design the component-based system architecture using React, define the two-chatbot routing structure specifying the landing page entry points and the shared chat UI component, and define the Supabase database schema supporting session-scoped assessment state, the curated facility directory, and the shared pgvector knowledge base table storing content chunks, their embeddings, source and provenance metadata, and the scope metadata that separates screening-clarification passages from general CKD education passages  
* Design the Rule-Based Screening Controller flow for the Risk Assessment Chatbot, specifying the sequential SCORED variable presentation logic, the mid-session delegation of clarification requests to the retrieval-augmented LLM Clarification Engine and the return of control to the current variable, and the session completion condition that triggers score computation, with the scoring path defined as fully deterministic and architecturally isolated from both the retrieval branch and the post-classification Facility Locator  
* Design the shared retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline serving both chatbots, specifying the chunking strategy, the embedding model, the provenance metadata fields required for source traceability, the scope metadata schema that logically separates the screening-clarification corpus from the general CKD education corpus, the similarity threshold and top-k retrieval parameters set independently for each scope, and the fallback behavior when no retrieved passage meets the threshold; define the system prompt structure for both chatbots as an answer-only-from-retrieved-context instruction, and specify the Edge Function–level scope guardrail governing refusal of out-of-scope and adversarial queries for the General CKD Chatbot  
* Design the Supabase Edge Function architecture that will perform query embedding, scope-filtered vector retrieval, facility proximity queries, and all LLM API calls securely server-side, with scope filtering applied as a structural constraint within the retrieval query rather than as an instruction issued to the language model  
* Define the source inclusion and exclusion criteria governing the knowledge base, specifying the three admissible source categories — official health organizations and government health agencies, clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements, and indexed peer-reviewed journal literature — together with the currency, attribution, and public-retrievability requirements, the exclusion of grey literature and non-attributable content, and the adviser approval step required before any source is ingested  
* Design the Facility Locator Module, specifying the schema of the curated facility directory, the digital map service integration, the proximity query logic, the location-permission flow and its manual city or municipality fallback, the facility disclaimer content, and the placement of the module as a post-classification branch that returns no value to the scoring or classification components  
* Produce UI wireframes for all major screens: landing page with dual chatbot entry points and facility locator access, informed consent screen, Risk Assessment Chatbot interface, General CKD Chatbot interface, results display with medical disclaimer, and the facility locator map view including its location-permission prompt and manual location fallback  
  Output: Approved system design documentation and wireframes  
  **Sprint 2: SCORED Risk Assessment Module**   
  This sprint will implement and unit-test the core scoring engine. Key tasks:  
* Implement the nine-variable SCORED scoring logic as a dedicated JavaScript service module within the React application, accepting the nine binary variable values as input and returning a cumulative risk score and classification  
* Apply weighted point values per Bang et al. (2007): age 50–59 (2 pts), age 60–69 (3 pts), age 70+ (4 pts), all other positive variables (1 pt each)  
* Implement binary classification: Screen Negative (0–3) and Screen Positive (≥4)  
* Write white-box unit tests covering all score boundary cases

		Output: A fully tested scoring module with a 100% unit test pass rate.

**Sprint 3: Chatbot Interfaces, Shared UI Component, and Results Display**

This sprint will develop the conversational front-end and the session-scoped results display. Key tasks:

* Build the shared React-based chat UI component that serves as the base interface for both chatbots, implementing conversational chat bubbles, structured response inputs, and free-form text entry, and integrate it into two distinct routes and page components — one for the Risk Assessment Chatbot and one for the General CKD Chatbot — with visual distinction between the two interfaces conveying the structured, goal-directed nature of the assessment flow versus the open-ended nature of the general CKD conversation  
* Implement the Rule-Based Screening Controller within the Risk Assessment Chatbot, governing the sequential presentation of all nine SCORED variables, detecting mid-session clarification requests and delegating them to the LLM Clarification Engine, and resuming the current variable after each clarification exchange  
* Implement the Supabase Edge Functions that perform query embedding, scope-filtered vector retrieval, and all LLM API calls securely server-side for both chatbots, ensuring that API credentials are never exposed in the client-side build; scaffold the retrieval pipeline against a placeholder vector table seeded with a small representative sample of content so that retrieval, scope filtering, answer-from-context behavior, and the no-qualifying-passage fallback can be verified end to end for both chatbots pending ingestion of the full curated knowledge base in Sprint 4  
* Implement the pre-screening instruction in the Risk Assessment Chatbot informing users that uncertain or inapplicable responses should be recorded as zero, and verify through testing that the LLM Clarification Engine retrieves correctly under the screening-clarification scope, responds using only retrieved content, and returns control to the Rule-Based Screening Controller following clarification requests for all nine SCORED variables  
* Implement real-time score computation and results display upon session completion of the Risk Assessment Chatbot  
* Implement session-scoped state handling so that assessment responses and computed results exist only for the duration of the active session and are discarded when the session ends, with no persistence of user-submitted responses or results to the database  
* Ensure full responsiveness across desktop and mobile web browsers for both chatbot interfaces

		Output: Two responsive chatbot interfaces built on a shared UI component.

**Sprint 4: Knowledge Base Ingestion, RAG Pipeline, Recommendation Engine, and Facility Locator**

This sprint will build the shared knowledge base, ingest it into the vector store, implement the retrieval pipeline that serves it to both chatbots, and build the logic that delivers classification-specific recommendations and nearby testing laboratory listings. Key tasks:

* Curate CKD educational content covering causes, symptoms, risk factors, prevention, and management, together with plain-language definitions of each of the nine SCORED variables intended for the screening-clarification scope, drawing on sources admitted under the source inclusion framework: official health organizations and government health agencies, clinical practice guidelines and consensus statements, and indexed peer-reviewed journal literature. Each candidate source is submitted for adviser approval and recorded in the source register before ingestion; where content is drawn from clinical guidelines or journal literature, it is simplified for lay comprehension while retaining a citation to its original source  
* Prepare the curated content as structured markdown documents, apply the chunking strategy defined in Sprint 1, generate embeddings for each chunk, and ingest the resulting vectors into the shared pgvector table in Supabase together with their source attribution and provenance metadata  
* Assign scope metadata to every ingested chunk, tagging screening-variable clarification content and general CKD education content distinctly, so that a single shared pipeline serves both chatbots while retrieval for each subsystem remains logically separated  
* Implement the scope-filtered retrieval function within the Supabase Edge Function layer, applying the per-scope similarity threshold and top-k values defined in Sprint 1 — with a stricter threshold and lower top-k applied to the screening-clarification scope given its proximity to the assessment flow — and a defined refusal response for cases where no retrieved passage meets the threshold  
* Retain the curated content records as the content pool from which the Recommendation Engine retrieves classification-specific output sets, kept separate from the retrieval path used by the chatbots  
* Organize recommendation content into two output sets corresponding to Screen Negative and Screen Positive classifications for delivery by the Recommendation Engine following assessment completion  
* Implement the Recommendation Engine using conditional logic to retrieve and display the appropriate content set based on the user's SCORED classification  
* Compile the curated facility directory for Davao Region (Region XI) by exporting records of the Clinical Laboratory facility type from the DOH National Health Facility Registry, retaining only facilities whose licensing status is current, and recording for each entry the health facility code, facility name, ownership classification, service capability level, address, barangay and its PSGC code, city or municipality, province, licensing status and validity date where published, and the snapshot capture date  
* Apply the service capability inclusion rule derived from Administrative Order No. 2021-0037, assigning each licensed record to one of three display tiers: a primary tier comprising Level 2 and Level 3 laboratories, for which routine clinical chemistry is a required service and which are displayed by default; a secondary tier comprising Level 1 laboratories, retained in the directory but displayed only when the user enables the disclosure toggle and always accompanied by an advisory that clinical chemistry is not a required service at that level; and an excluded tier comprising records with no published service capability and records carrying a drug testing screening licence, which are omitted entirely as they may not be general clinical laboratories  
* Build the Facility Locator results interface with two display tiers: laboratories of Level 2 and Level 3 service capability shown by default, and a user-controlled toggle labelled “Also show laboratories where creatinine testing is not a required service” which, when enabled, additionally displays Level 1 laboratories. Each Level 1 result carries an inline advisory stating that routine clinical chemistry is not a required service at that level and that the laboratory should be contacted before visiting, with the facility's telephone number or email address surfaced alongside the advisory where the registry records one, and an explicit statement where it records neither  
* Derive geographic coordinates for every directory entry, as the registry does not publish them, by joining each record on its ten-digit PSGC code to a barangay boundary dataset built from NAMRIA administrative-boundary shapefiles and the PSA Philippine Standard Geographic Code, dissolving multi-part barangays by code and computing a representative point guaranteed to fall within each barangay rather than a mathematical centroid; retain the match status, match confidence and part count reported by the source dataset against every record for auditability, and verify a sample of the resulting coordinates by manual spot-check before ingestion  
* Implement the Facility Locator Module, integrating a digital map service to render nearby facilities, resolving the user's approximate location only through an explicit browser geolocation permission prompt at the point of use, providing manual city or municipality entry as an equivalent alternative, and returning results ranked by proximity  
* Implement the out-of-coverage response across three cases: users whose resolved location falls outside Region XI, for whom the system states that directory coverage is currently limited to Davao Region; users within Region XI whose municipality contains no primary-tier laboratory but does contain a secondary-tier laboratory, for whom the system prompts the disclosure toggle rather than reporting nothing; and users whose municipality contains neither, for whom the system reports the nearest laboratories in adjacent municipalities. In no case does the system return an empty result set without explanation  
* Embed the facility disclaimer stating that the listing is informational, that it does not constitute an endorsement or clinical referral, that facility data is current as of the displayed snapshot date, and that users should confirm test availability and operating hours directly with the facility before travelling  
* Embed the medical disclaimer within both output sets  
* Finalize and deploy the system prompts for both chatbots as answer-only-from-retrieved-context instructions, with explicit refusal behavior where retrieval returns no qualifying passage, and enable the Edge Function–level scope guardrail for the General CKD Chatbot, now that the shared vector knowledge base is fully ingested and queryable  
  Output: A populated shared vector knowledge base carrying provenance and scope metadata, a working scope-filtered retrieval pipeline serving both chatbots, a functional Recommendation Engine, and a working Facility Locator backed by the curated facility directory.  
  **Sprint 5: Data Privacy, Security, and Ethical Safeguards**   
  This sprint will implement all data protection, privacy, and ethical system features. Key tasks:  
* Implement session-scoped data handling in place of user registration and authentication, verifying that no personally identifiable information is collected at any point and that assessment responses and results are discarded when the session ends, consistent with the data minimization principle of Republic Act No. 10173  
* Enforce HTTPS for all data transmission and configure Supabase Row Level Security (RLS) policies so that the shared knowledge base and the curated facility directory are read-only from the client and reachable only through the Edge Function layer, with no client-side write path and no publicly queryable table containing user-submitted content  
* Implement an informed consent screen presented before the assessment begins, explaining the purpose of the screening, the voluntary nature of participation, that no personally identifiable information is collected and no account is required, and that responses are held only for the duration of the session and are discarded when it ends  
* Configure access control on the shared vector knowledge base so that it is readable only through the Supabase Edge Functions using a server-side service role, with no direct client-side query path to the vector table  
* Verify that the scope filter is applied server-side on every retrieval call for both chatbots and cannot be overridden or widened by user input, and that no user-supplied text is interpolated into the retrieval query in a manner capable of altering the scope filter  
* Implement the location-permission flow for the Facility Locator, requesting device location only at the point of use through explicit user action, providing manual location entry as an equivalent alternative for users who decline, and ensuring that location input is used solely to generate the current result set and is written neither to the database nor to application logs  
* Display a prominent medical disclaimer on the results screen clarifying that BATO is a screening tool and not a clinical diagnostic instrument, and that Screen Positive users should seek professional medical evaluation  
* Ensure no personally identifiable health data is shared with third parties  
  Output: A secured, ethically compliant system operating without user accounts, with informed consent, location-permission, and disclaimer mechanisms in place.  
  **Sprint 6: Testing and Refinement**   
  This sprint will conduct comprehensive system evaluation and resolve all identified issues. Key tasks:  
* White-box testing of the SCORED Scoring Engine against all boundary cases per Bang et al. (2007), covering all score boundary values, all four age bracket point assignments, and all binary variable combinations producing scores at the Screen Negative/Screen Positive threshold  
* Black-box functional testing of both chatbot subsystems and the Facility Locator using a structured checklist covering all major features, including Rule-Based Screening Controller sequencing, LLM Clarification Engine delegation and resumption behavior, retrieval correctness and scope isolation for both chatbots, refusal behavior where retrieval returns no qualifying passage, General CKD Chatbot scope guardrail enforcement against off-topic and prompt-injection inputs, Recommendation Engine output correctness, Facility Locator proximity results together with its location-permission and manual-entry paths, informed consent screen, medical and facility disclaimer display, and verification that no assessment response or result persists after the session ends  
* Black-box verification of the Facility Locator display tiers, covering the default view showing primary-tier laboratories only, correct behaviour of the disclosure toggle in both states, presence of the service capability advisory on every secondary-tier result, correct surfacing of a telephone number or email address where the registry records one and an explicit statement where it records neither, and correct handling of all three out-of-coverage cases  
* Retrieval evaluation of the shared RAG pipeline using a fixed question set defined per scope, recording for each query whether the retrieved passages are relevant, whether the generated response is fully supported by those passages, and whether any cross-scope leakage occurs in either direction; confirm in particular that no screening-clarification query returns a response capable of influencing the value recorded for a SCORED variable  
* Usability testing using the System Usability Scale (SUS) with a minimum of 20 Filipino adult participants aged 20 and above, recruited through purposive sampling to represent a range of digital literacy levels  
* User acceptance evaluation using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) instrument to assess participants' perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of the BATO system  
* Medical trust evaluation using the Trust in Medical Technology (TiMT) instrument to assess participants' level of trust in BATO as a health screening tool  
* Post-session comprehension check consisting of two to three short questions verifying that the participant understood their screening result, the meaning of that result, and the recommended next action  
* Document, fix, and confirm resolution of all identified issues across both chatbot subsystems  
  Output: A fully tested and refined system with documented evaluation results across white-box, black-box, SUS, TAM, TiMT, and comprehension check instruments.  
  **Sprint 7: Deployment**  
  This sprint will prepare and execute the deployment of the fully tested BATO system to a live web hosting environment. Key tasks:  
* Configure the production hosting environment for the React build, ensuring connectivity to the Supabase project and HTTPS enforcement, and verify that all Supabase environment variables are correctly set for the production context  
* Finalize environment-specific configuration, including production-grade Supabase API keys and RLS policies, and confirm that all LLM API, embedding, and map service credentials are secured server-side and are not exposed in the client-side build  
* Deploy the system to a publicly accessible web server with a domain or subdomain assigned for user testing and final evaluation  
* Conduct smoke testing on the live environment to verify that all features function correctly post-deployment, with particular attention to chatbot interaction and retrieval, score computation, results display, and Facility Locator behavior across both the location-permission and manual-entry paths  
* Finalize the source register as of submission, recording every source ingested into the knowledge base, its category under the source inclusion framework, its publication or revision year, and the date of adviser approval  
* Resolve any environment-specific issues identified during smoke testing before releasing the system for user access  
  Output: A live, publicly accessible deployment of BATO ready for user evaluation.  
  **Sprint 8: Review**  
  This sprint will conduct a structured post-deployment review of the entire development process and system performance, serving as the formal closing phase of the Agile cycle. Key tasks:  
* Evaluate outcomes of all preceding sprints against the four study objectives and document the extent to which each objective was met  
* Consolidate findings from white-box testing, black-box testing, SUS usability evaluation, TAM user acceptance evaluation, TiMT medical trust evaluation, and the post-session comprehension check into a formal evaluation report  
* Document lessons learned throughout the development process, including technical challenges, design revisions, and identified areas for future improvement  
* Formally note the handling of proteinuria under user uncertainty as a priority limitation and direction for future development  
* Document the delimitations of the Facility Locator directory, namely that it covers Region XI only, this being the sole region in which the National Health Facility Registry publishes laboratory service capability at a completeness sufficient to apply the inclusion rule; that inclusion is determined by published service capability rather than by confirmation from each facility, so that no laboratory in either display tier has been individually verified as currently performing serum creatinine testing; that Level 1 laboratories which do in fact offer the test are shown only behind the disclosure toggle while laboratories with no published capability are omitted entirely; that coordinates are resolved at barangay level and therefore indicate the locality rather than the exact premises of a facility; that the barangay boundaries from which those coordinates are computed are simplified at a tolerance of approximately 550 metres and are therefore generalised rather than surveyed; and that the boundary and code snapshots date to late 2023 while the facility registry extract dates to 2026, such that barangays created or recoded in the interval may not resolve on a future refresh; and that two laboratories whose registered names indicate a drug testing service were excluded as a precaution despite carrying a Level 2 service capability, on the basis that their published name is inconsistent with general clinical laboratory service; and that the directory reflects the registry as of the snapshot capture date, with subsequent licensing changes not represented;   
* Produce final system documentation required for Capstone 2 submission, including updated technical specifications, user testing results, and a summary of system performance against the study's acceptance criteria  
* Record national expansion of the facility directory as a direction for future work, noting that the compilation pipeline is region-agnostic and that extending coverage beyond Region XI requires only a re-run of the registry export and centroid join at such time as the Department of Health populates laboratory service capability in additional regions  
  Output: A completed evaluation report and final system documentation marking the conclusion of the Capstone 2 development phase.  
3. **Testing Procedure**  
   The testing strategy for BATO will employ three complementary approaches applied at different layers of the system.  
   **White-Box Testing**  
   White-box testing will be applied to the SCORED scoring engine to verify that the internal logic produces outputs consistent with Bang et al. (2007). Test cases will cover all score boundary values, all four age bracket point assignments, and all binary variable combinations producing scores at the Screen Negative/Screen Positive threshold (scores 3 and 4). The engine will be approved for integration only upon achieving a 100% pass rate.  
   **Black-Box Testing**

**![][image4]**

*Figure 4: Black \- Box Testing*

Black-box functional testing will be conducted on both chatbot subsystems as a complete integrated system. Testers will interact with BATO as end users without access to source code, evaluating whether each feature behaves as expected using a structured checklist.

For the Risk Assessment Chatbot, coverage will include: informed consent screen display; pre-screening instruction display; Rule-Based Screening Controller sequencing — verifying that all nine SCORED variables are presented in the correct order, that mid-session clarification requests are correctly delegated to the LLM Clarification Engine which retrieves under the screening-clarification scope and returns a plain-language response supported entirely by the retrieved passages, that the engine declines to answer where no retrieved passage meets the similarity threshold rather than generating unsupported content, and that control reliably returns to the current SCORED variable after each clarification exchange without alteration to any previously recorded response; score computation correctness upon session completion; risk classification display; Recommendation Engine output correctness for both Screen Negative and Screen Positive results; Facility Locator behavior, including the location-permission prompt, the manual city or municipality fallback for users who decline permission, proximity ranking, map rendering, and facility disclaimer display; medical disclaimer display; and verification that assessment responses and results do not persist once the session ends.

For the General CKD Chatbot, coverage will include: correct acceptance and response to CKD-related queries; scope guardrail enforcement — verifying that off-topic queries and adversarial prompt-injection attempts are declined at the Edge Function layer before retrieval or generation occurs; retrieval and source-grounding behavior — verifying that each response is supported by the passages retrieved from the approved source corpus, that every claim is traceable to its source document, and that the system declines to answer where no retrieved passage meets the similarity threshold; and scope isolation — verifying that general CKD education retrieval does not return screening-clarification passages and that the reverse does not occur.

**Usability Testing and System Effectiveness Measure**

Usability testing will be conducted with a minimum of twenty (20) Filipino adult participants aged 20 and above, recruited through purposive sampling to represent a range of digital literacy levels. Each participant will complete a full BATO session — including interaction with the Risk Assessment Chatbot, use of the Facility Locator following the screening result, and, where time permits, the General CKD Chatbot — followed by three evaluation instruments administered in sequence.

The first instrument is the System Usability Scale (SUS), which will measure the overall perceived usability of the BATO system. A mean SUS score of 68 or above will be considered the minimum acceptable threshold, with scores above 80 indicating excellent usability.

The second instrument is the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaire, which will assess participants' perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of BATO as a health screening and information tool. TAM responses will be recorded on a five-point Likert scale and analyzed to determine the degree to which participants found the system useful and easy to engage with in the context of CKD risk awareness.

The third instrument is the Trust in Medical Technology (TiMT) questionnaire, which will assess participants' level of trust in BATO as a technology-based health screening tool. TiMT responses will provide a quantifiable indicator of whether participants considered BATO's outputs credible and appropriate as a basis for health-related decisions, which is of particular relevance given that BATO's LLM-generated responses are grounded in institutionally approved health authority content.

To measure system effectiveness, a brief post-session comprehension check will be administered immediately after each participant completes the Risk Assessment Chatbot session. This check will consist of two to three short questions verifying that the participant understood their screening result (Screen Negative or Screen Positive), the meaning of that result, the recommended next action, and — for participants classified as Screen Positive — where they may go to obtain confirmatory testing. Correct responses will be recorded as a percentage of total participants, providing a simple and quantifiable indicator of whether BATO successfully communicated its screening outcome to its target users.
